summary:
Multi Lunar Labs is an educational game developed in GDevelop by Golondrinas Espaciales for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. It invites students to train as junior astronauts and discover what it takes to keep a base running at the Moon’s south pole.
Players manage the rover’s battery while collecting anorthosite and lunar breccia samples. Back at the base, they examine the rocks with a simulated X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer and assemble a life support system that recovers water, cleans the air, and generates oxygen.
The game also connects life support with food production. In a greenhouse inspired by potato-growing research with soil from La Joya, Arequipa, Peru, players use recovered water to grow potatoes. The harvest then goes to the 3D food printing lab, where potato purée is shaped into portions for the crew.
Through these missions, students explore, make decisions about limited resources, and see how the systems of a lunar base depend on one another.
details:
Project Details

1. How the game works
Multi Lunar Labs is an educational game that lets students train as junior astronauts at the Moon’s south pole. Players manage the rover’s battery, collect anorthosite and lunar breccia samples, and examine them with a simulated X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer. Inside the base, they assemble a life support system that recovers water, cleans the air, and generates oxygen. The game connects this system to food production: recovered water irrigates potatoes, and the harvest supplies the 3D food printing lab.

2. Educational benefits and intended impact
We designed the game to help young learners explore, make decisions, and understand how the systems of a lunar base depend on one another. A limited rover battery gives players a reason to plan their route, while the greenhouse shows why recovering water matters. We want students to see how science and engineering help solve practical problems and feel curious enough to keep exploring them.

3. Tools and scientific sources
We built the game in GDevelop, using its visual event system to program rover movement, resource counters, drag-and-drop interactions, animations, and scene transitions. We used ChatGPT Plus to generate custom visual assets, including backgrounds, equipment, and sprites, which we integrated into the game. We used NASA’s published documentation on the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) to design the life support module and NASA-funded research to inform the food printing lab. The greenhouse also draws on potato-growing research using soil from La Joya, Arequipa, Peru.

4. What makes the project creative
We turned scientific and engineering concepts into tasks students can perform themselves. Players assemble life support equipment piece by piece, see the indicator lights turn green, and follow the recovered water from the ECLSS to the potato crop. When designing these missions, we considered limited resources, clear instructions, and how to simplify complex processes for young players while preserving the connections between them.
